title: Exercise the mind
hookLine: short, simple exercise for the body, then back to the mind

lines: IF YOU ARE WELL, IT IS WELL.
IF YOU DO PHILOSOPHY, IT IS WELL.
cards: The old Romans, Seneca says, had a custom that lasted into his own lifetime: they opened a letter with a little formula. If you are well, it is well; I am well.
Seneca opens his fifteenth letter by recalling that greeting, then changes it. If you're doing philosophy, he writes, it is well. Without it, the mind is sick, and that's no kind of being well.
And then, a little unexpectedly, he spends the letter on the gym.

teach.h: A SOUND MIND, NOT ONLY A BODY.
teach.b: For Seneca, a strong body around a neglected mind isn't health at all. The mind needs its own training, every day. He isn't against the body, though.
He's against overdoing it. He pokes fun at people who spend all day building huge muscles and thick necks, eating and drinking to bulk up, taking orders from trainers.

teach.h: NO NEED TO MATCH A PRIZE BULL.
teach.b: However big you get, he says, you'll never match a prize bull. And all that heavy training tires the mind out, too.
So he recommends quick, simple exercises: running, swinging hand weights, jumping, even a kind of hopping dance the Salian priests did in processions.

teach.h: RUN, SWING, JUMP, WALK, READ ALOUD.
teach.b: A jolting ride in a litter is fine too, since it doesn't stop you studying, and so is reading aloud, for the voice and the breath. The rule: whatever you do, come back quickly from the body to the mind.

teach.h: THE MIND TRAINS DAY AND NIGHT.
teach.b: The mind should be exercised day and night, and it needs no good weather or special equipment. A little work keeps it fed. Cold, heat and old age can't stop it.
Not lazy for the body. Brief. Someone who sits at a desk all day may need more movement than Seneca's short list.
His point still stands: train both, and don't let the smaller one eat the bigger one's day.

how: Following Seneca, some people keep their physical exercise short and simple, often a walk, and use it as a lead-in to thinking, reading or reflection.

priests who read letters aloud in the temple
priests whose hopping dance was quick exercise

s: Seneca told Lucilius to skip exercise entirely
he recommends short, simple exercise, then a quick return to the mind.
Seneca says cold, heat or old age can stop the mind's training
he says the mind's exercise isn't hindered by cold, heat or even old age.
Seneca recommends reading aloud as a kind of exercise
he lists it among the light exercises, for the voice and the breath.

games.q: you're Lucilius, and you've started spending hours lifting heavy weights every day. what does Seneca advise?
o: keep going: the bigger the better.
keep it short and simple, then get back to your mind.
give up the body and only read.
games.why: he says you'll never match a prize bull anyway: train the body briefly, and the mind day and night.

practice: Stand up if you can and move for a few breaths: roll your shoulders, march in place, reach high and let your arms fall, or, if standing isn't possible, stretch your hands and neck gently.
Then sit, let the body be still, and turn over one question you've been carrying with a fresh, warm mind.

wordCard.voice: Salian priests. Their hopping dance in processions is one of the quick, simple exercises Seneca recommends before returning to the mind. Today's word.
